# Introduction: A New Kind of Computer Program {.unnumbered}

For the first time since the dawn of computer programming, there is a fundamentally new kind of computer program.

One that can apply judgment to messy inputs and use tools to take action: import contacts, draft and send emails, write files, deploy code. That’s useful—and dangerous. If you rely on the model to always call the right tool at the right time with the right inputs, you’re giving a monkey a razor blade and hoping for the best.

Since the 1950s, programming has meant one thing: anticipate every scenario and write code to handle it. Parse this format. Catch that error. Map these fields to those fields. If you miss a case, the program breaks.

That's changing.

## The Old Way: Think of Everything

Consider something as simple as importing contact data. A customer sends you a spreadsheet of contacts to add to your system.

The traditional approach requires you to think of everything.

Even if you restrict yourself to *one* contact record and *one* format (CSV), you still end up handling lots of variants. For example, all of these are “the same contact”, but with different headers and name formatting:

```text
First Name,Last Name,E-mail,Notes
FIRST,LAST,contact@example.com,VIP
```

```text
name,email,Notes
"LAST, FIRST",contact@example.com,VIP
```

```text
nombre,apellido,correo,notas
FIRST,LAST,contact@example.com,VIP
```

To handle even just these variations, you start writing code like this:

```python
import csv
from io import StringIO

from my_crm import file_contact  # Your CRM client (implementation not shown)


def import_contact(raw_contact: str):
    # Expect a 1-row CSV string (header + row).
    row = next(csv.DictReader(StringIO(raw_contact)), None)
    if not row:
        raise ValueError("No contact row found")

    # Email column mapping
    email = (
        row.get("email")
        or row.get("e-mail")
        or row.get("correo")
        or row.get("e mail")
    )
    if not email:
        raise ValueError("Could not find email column")

    # Name column mapping + normalization
    if row.get("name"):
        full = row["name"].strip()
        if "," in full:  # "Last, First"
            last_name, first_name = [p.strip() for p in full.split(",", 1)]
        else:            # "First Last"
            first_name, last_name = full.split(" ", 1)
    elif row.get("First Name") and row.get("Last Name"):
        first_name, last_name = row["First Name"], row["Last Name"]
    elif row.get("nombre") and row.get("apellido"):
        first_name, last_name = row["nombre"], row["apellido"]
    else:
        raise ValueError("Could not find name columns")

    notes = row.get("Notes") or row.get("notas") or ""

    return file_contact(
        first_name=first_name,
        last_name=last_name,
        email=email,
        notes=notes,
    )
```

This handles a few CSV variations. Each new variation means new code. The import function grows. Edge cases multiply. And still, the next file will have something you didn't anticipate.

## The New Way: Give an Agent a Tool

The agent-based approach inverts the problem.

Instead of writing code to handle every case, you define a capability—a tool—and describe what you want. The agent figures out how to use the tool to achieve the goal.

Here's the same idea in Tactus. Assume your application has already exposed a `file_contact` tool with typed inputs (`first_name`, `last_name`, `email`, `notes`). We'll define tools soon. (For a runnable version that defines a local stub tool, see `code/chapter-01/02-intro-contact-import.tac`.)

```lua {file="code/chapter-01/02-intro-contact-import.tac" snippet="intro-snippet" show-path="true"}
```

That's it. You exposed a capability (`file_contact`), gave it to the agent, and made a single agent call that results in a tool call.

When the columns are `nombre` and `correo`, the agent maps them. When names are `Last, First`, it parses them. New formats arrive? The agent adapts—without you adding a new pile of conditionals.

Now zoom out: in real systems, the “contact record” might not be a clean CSV row at all. You might get a JSON blob from an API, or someone pastes an email header into a support form. The Python approach needs new parsers; the agent-based version uses the same orchestration code:

```json
{
  "nombre": "FIRST",
  "apellido": "LAST",
  "correo": "contact@example.com",
  "notas": "VIP"
}
```

```text
From: "FIRST LAST" <contact@example.com>
Subject: New contact
X-Notes: VIP
```

That's the whole trick: if you give an agent a tool, then nobody has to fish.

This is what we call **"Give an Agent a Tool."** You're not writing code to handle cases—you're providing a capability and describing intent. The intelligence handles the variations.

## A Language for This New Paradigm

If you could just give an agent a set of tools and trust it to do the right thing, you'd be done. That's essentially what happens when you use Claude Code or Cursor with MCP tools—you describe what you want, provide some capabilities, and hope for the best.

It works pretty well, actually. When you're there.

The reason interactive tools work is that you're guiding the agent constantly. You can disapprove when it tries to call the wrong tool. You can abort when something goes sideways. You can redirect when it wanders off course. The human in the loop is doing a lot of implicit correction.

But when you're not there—when you need agents to run autonomously at scale—"hope for the best" falls apart. AI models don't follow instructions perfectly every time. Run the same agent a thousand times and even clear instructions will fail occasionally. At scale, small failure rates compound into real problems.

There's been evolution in this direction. Claude Code skills, for example, bundle tools with instructions for how to use them—a step toward structured guidance. Tactus takes this further: actual imperative programming for combining an agent with a specific set of tools, context, and instructions, then sending it off to do work.

Years of operating mission-critical systems, machine learning models, and agent-based automations taught us you need a middle ground. Not traditional programming where you anticipate every scenario. Not pure agent-based where you hope for the best. Something in between.

The solution is creating narrow, well-defined scenarios where agents apply their intelligence effectively:

- Give agents **only the tools they need** for each specific task
- Provide **only the context** needed for a specific decision
- **Break complex tasks** into smaller, focused pieces
- **Manage the information flow** between task executions
- **Change instructions** as the workflow progresses

In computer security, this is the **principle of least privilege**: give an actor the smallest set of capabilities and information it needs to do its job, for the shortest time, and nothing more. Tactus makes that practical for AI agents by letting you grant tools and context per stage (and even per turn), instead of running with a permanent, always-on toolbelt.

## Beyond Chat: Embedded Agent Programs

Chat is a fantastic interface for *developing* an agent. It’s often a poor interface for *using* one.

Most applications have common workflows that repeat: import a file, draft an email, triage a ticket, propose changes, ship a release. If every run requires a back-and-forth chat session, you’re asking users to engage deeply with the process—even when they just want to provide a missing field or approve a risky step.

Tactus is designed to be embedded into applications so agent programs can interact with users through **structured requests** at the right times:

- request missing information with `Human.input({ ... })`
- request a review (and allow edits) with `Human.review({ ... })`
- request approval before irreversible actions with `Human.approve({ ... })`
- emit high-level stages, logs, and traces for monitoring and operations

That’s why HITL is a set of language primitives rather than a framework convention: the procedure declares **what** it needs, and the host application decides **how** to render it—CLI prompts, web modals, Slack messages, email links, or your own UI components.

Durability makes this practical. When a procedure reaches a HITL call, it can suspend indefinitely without keeping a process alive. When the human responds hours (or days) later, the procedure resumes from that checkpoint—potentially in a fresh process, on a different machine, in a different runtime environment.

## From Prototypes to Reproducible Procedures

Tools like Claude Code and Cursor (and features like Claude’s skills) are great for prototyping. They work because a developer is present: supervising, steering, and ensuring the model uses the right tools in the right order.

But that doesn’t package well—especially for non-developers.

Tactus procedures are runnable artifacts. They encode the setup steps deterministically (including “run tool X first”), keep capabilities explicit, and expose a typed interface (`input`/`output`) that other people can run like a program. A subject-matter expert doesn’t need to babysit a chat session—they can approve, review, or provide missing inputs at durable checkpoints.

One way to see the shift is as a set of control surfaces. Prompts are one lever—but they’re the softest. As you’ll see later in this book (Part III), Tactus is designed to give you stronger, more enforceable leverage “below” the prompt layer:

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
  MB["Model behavior<br/>(prompts, examples, model choice)"]
  OC["Orchestration code<br/>(procedures, stages, checks)"]
  Capabilities["Capabilities<br/>(tools + context, principle of least privilege)"]
  Isolation["Isolation boundaries<br/>(Lua VM, containers, brokers)"]
  Humans["Humans<br/>(approve, review, input)"]
  Feedback["Feedback<br/>(logs, traces, specs, evals)"]
  MB --> OC --> Capabilities --> Isolation --> Humans --> Feedback
```

A new programming paradigm also requires a new testing paradigm.

Traditional programming is deterministic—run the same code twice, get the same result. You can write unit tests that pass or fail. Agent-based programming is non-deterministic. The question isn't just "does it produce the right answer?" but "does it *reliably* produce the right answer?" Those are different questions, and they require different testing approaches.

Python comes with unittest. Ruby has its testing frameworks. Tactus has testing built in for an agent-based world—which means not just behavioral specifications (does the code do what it should?) but also evaluations (how often does it succeed?). This combines behavior-driven development from software engineering with evaluation methodology from machine learning.

Tactus is a programming language that makes all of this manageable. The hybrid approach to orchestration. The testing philosophy for non-deterministic systems. All without writing huge amounts of infrastructure code.

The language handles the concerns that this new kind of program requires:

- **Tool Management**: Control exactly which tools an agent can access at any moment
- **Context Engineering**: Shape what information an agent sees for each decision
- **Durability**: Agent programs run for hours or days, surviving crashes and restarts
- **Human-in-the-Loop**: Agents pause for human approval or guidance mid-execution
- **A New Testing Paradigm**: BDD specifications for behavior, evaluations for reliability
- **Compact Code**: Definitions small enough for AI coding agents to read and modify

This book will teach you to write this new kind of program.

## The Tactus Workflow: Spec First

In this book, testing isn't a later chapter—it's how you write Tactus from the beginning.

When you start a new `.tac` procedure:

1. Write a `Specifications([[ ... ]])` block that describes the behavior you want in plain language.
2. Add `Mocks { ... }` for any external tools (and, later, DSPy modules) so you can iterate quickly and deterministically.
3. Run `tactus test yourfile.tac --mock` until the workflow logic is correct.
4. Switch to real mode (`tactus test yourfile.tac`) and then run multiple times (`tactus test yourfile.tac --runs 10`) to measure reliability.

A practical trick is to run once in real mode, then copy the tool/module outputs you observed into your `Mocks` block so future runs are fast and deterministic. Tactus already records every call for durability, so turning a “real run” into a reusable mock fixture is a natural workflow—even if you do it manually at first.

For a deterministic spec-first example you can run entirely in mock mode, see `code/chapter-05/02-basics-simple-logic.tac`. For the `Mocks { ... }` syntax itself, see `code/chapter-05/70-mocking-static.tac`.
